11224139_ff5d45fb.text: In the rodent dLGN, there appears to be just one type of interneuron (Acuña-Goycolea et al., 2008)[16](Williams et al., 1996). The dLGN is a vital link in the visual pathway from the eye to the visual cortex [16,18]. Retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) activate thalamocortical (TC) neurons that convey visually evoked signals to the cortex, and local interneurons within the dLGN that provide feedforward inhibition to TC cells. dLGN interneurons control the number of visually evoked spikes, regulate the precision of firing, and refine the receptive fields (RFs) of TC neurons (Berardi et al., 1984)(Blitz et al., 2005)(Usrey et al., 1999)(Sillito et al., 1983) (Norton et al., 1992)(Norton et al., 1989)

11224139_4166977c.text: .dLGN interneurons release GABA from both their axons and dendrites [16](Cox et al., 1998). Their dendrites support both brief sodium action potentials and longlasting calcium spikes, whereas their axons support only sodium spikes. Thus, active responses in the postsynaptic cell control the magnitude, spatial properties and time course of GABA release.
